warmup.q: A test runs backgroundScope.launch { gateway.events().collect { got += it } }, where events() is a correct callbackFlow that registers a listener, and on the very next line calls gateway.fire(event). Then it calls runCurrent(). What is in got?
options: Nothing: the listener wasn't registered when the event fired
warmup.why: On the default StandardTestDispatcher, launch only queues the collector. The callbackFlow block that calls register runs in a producer coroutine when the scheduler next runs, which is at runCurrent(), after the fire. The event found no listener and went nowhere. Production code has the same gap.

sections.h: A callbackFlow is a mailbox bolted to the SDK
sections.html:
Here is a bridge from a payment gateway's listener API to a Flow. The caller starts collecting, yields once, and then the gateway fires an event:

Java
// Java equivalent: Flux.create runs its lambda inside subscribe(), so the listener is there at once
Flux<PayEvent> events = Flux.create(sink -> {
    PayRegistration registration = gateway.register(new PayListener() {
        public void onEvent(PayEvent e) { sink.next(e); }
        public void onError(Throwable t) { sink.error(t); }
        public void onClosed() { sink.complete(); }
    });
    sink.onDispose(registration::unregister);
});
events.subscribe(e -> System.out.println("got " + e));
gateway.fire(new PayEvent("p-0", "AUTHORIZED"));   // got PayEvent(paymentId=p-0, ...)
Kotlin
fun DemoGateway.events(): Flow<PayEvent> = callbackFlow {
    val registration = register(object : PayListener {
        override fun onEvent(event: PayEvent) { trySend(event) }   // on the SDK's thread
        override fun onError(error: Throwable) { close(error) }
        override fun onClosed() { close() }
    })
    awaitClose { registration.unregister() }
}

launch { gateway.events().collect { println("got $it") } }
yield()
gateway.fire(PayEvent("p-0", "AUTHORIZED"))   // fired with listeners=0

The Kotlin event is lost. collect on a callbackFlow starts a producer coroutine, and your block, with its register call, runs inside that coroutine when it is first scheduled. launch and one yield() got the collector going, but not its producer. Reactor's Flux.create runs its lambda inside subscribe(), on the calling thread, so the Java version has no gap. In Kotlin, collecting does not mean registered. A test must wait for the registration, and production code must not count on it.

Picture the bridge as a mailbox bolted to the SDK's front door. The SDK's thread drops each event through the slot with trySend, which never blocks. send would wait for room, so it is a suspend function, and calling it from a plain listener method doesn't compile: "suspension functions can only be called within coroutine body". awaitClose { } is you sitting on the porch until you're told to leave, then unscrewing the mailbox. It suspends until the channel closes and runs its block in a finally, so the listener goes away whatever ended the flow: take(2), a cancelled collector, close(error) from onError (the collector's collect throws that error), or close() from onClosed (the flow completes normally).

Forget awaitClose, and the library sounds an alarm as soon as the block returns with the channel still open:

java.lang.IllegalStateException: 'awaitClose { yourCallbackOrListener.cancel() }' should be used in the end of callbackFlow block.
Otherwise, a callback/listener may leak in case of external cancellation.
See callbackFlow API documentation for the details.

Reactor has no such check. A Flux.create without onDispose still has its listener registered after take(1) has finished, and nothing tells you. For your own coroutines feeding one flow, such as quotes from two acquirers that you launch, use channelFlow, the same machinery without the check: it completes when the block and all its children are done. For a callback that fires once, use suspendCancellableCoroutine.

Parts 2 to 4 each print unregistered: after take(2) with the first two events, before the collector catches IOException: gateway connection lost, and when the flow completes with the REFUNDED event. Part 5 shows trySend on a closed channel: isSuccess=false isClosed=true. video.title: callbackFlow is a mailbox bolted to the SDK: the listener drops events in with trySend, awaitClose unregisters it, a burst of 200 gets 64 slots plus one waiting hand, and in tests advanceTimeBy(100) stops just before a task due at 100

sections.h: A burst of 200: 64 slots and one waiting hand
sections.html:
On connect, many SDKs replay what you missed in one synchronous burst. Fire 200 events into a default callbackFlow while its collector waits in receive(), and 135 trySend calls fail. The other 65 got through: 64 into the channel's buffer (Channel.BUFFERED), and one handed straight to the receiver that was already waiting, before the buffer was touched. So a buffer of 64 accepts 65 when a receiver is waiting. Better to know that before a test counts it for you.

trySend returns a ChannelResult. Ignore it, and the 135 failures are silent loss. After the channel is closed it fails too, with isClosed=true. The fix is a policy you choose on purpose. A buffer(...) or conflate() right after callbackFlow { } is fused into its one channel (lesson 4 of this track), so it changes that channel instead of adding a second one:

After callbackFlow { } trySend failures The collector got
nothing (64, SUSPEND) 135 65 accepted
.buffer(Channel.UNLIMITED) 0 all 200
.conflate() 0 [0, 199]: the first went to the waiting receiver, the last stayed in the one slot
.buffer(10, DROP_OLDEST) 0 [0, 190, 191, ..., 199]
Java
// Java equivalent: Flux.create buffers without limit by default (OverflowStrategy.BUFFER);
// onBackpressureBuffer(500) caps it and fails with an overflow error past 500
Flux<PayEvent> events = Flux.create(sink -> { /* register, sink.next, onDispose */ })
    .onBackpressureBuffer(500);
Kotlin
fun DemoGateway.events(): Flow<PayEvent> = callbackFlow { /* register, trySend, awaitClose */ }
    .buffer(500)   // fused: the bridge's own channel now holds the documented 500-event replay

trySendBlocking(e) looks like the safe version. It is trySend with a fallback of runBlocking { send(e) }, so when the buffer is full it blocks the SDK's own thread until there is room. With an SDK thread pushing 200 events and a collector that takes 2 ms each, trySend let the thread finish at once and lost 135, while trySendBlocking lost none and held the SDK thread for about 300 ms. (That run is real time, so your numbers will differ.) Use it only when the SDK runs your callback on a worker thread of its own and blocking that thread is how you push back. Pick UNLIMITED only when the producer is bounded. For a feed where only the latest status matters, conflate() drops in a way you can explain.

In part 2, trySend lets the SDK thread finish almost at once with about 135 failures, and the collector receives about 65. trySendBlocking holds the SDK thread for about 300 ms and loses nothing. sections.h: Across the Reactor bridge, demand becomes suspension
sections.html:
Reactive Streams makes the subscriber say how much it can take, with request(n). A Flow has no such call: it suspends. The bridges in kotlinx-coroutines-reactive and -reactor translate one into the other.

Publisher.asFlow() works like a diner with an order pad. It requests 64, eats them, then requests 64 more after every 64 it has passed downstream. (A Flux is a Publisher, so flux.asFlow() is this same function.) The elements wait in a channel of that size, and buffer sets the size of the order:

Flow side Requests sent to a 300-item Flux
asFlow() 64 after 0, 64, 128, 192 and 256
asFlow().buffer(10) 10 every 10
asFlow().buffer(0) 1 every 1
asFlow().conflate() or .buffer(UNLIMITED) Long.MAX_VALUE, once
asFlow().take(3) 64, then cancel: the 61 extra already in the channel are thrown away

That is a batch refill. Reactor's own operators top up earlier: publishOn asked a Flow-backed Flux for 256 and then 192 at a time, and limitRate(10) for 10 and then 8.

Flow.asFlux() and asPublisher() go the other way. Nothing runs until the first request(n). Then each emit calls onNext right there, inside emit, and counts the demand down. When it reaches 0, the flow suspends inside that emit, and a later request resumes it. After request(2) the subscriber had [1, 2], and emit had returned only for 1: the flow was parked inside emit(2). Cancelling the subscription cancels the flow's coroutine, so a callbackFlow underneath runs its awaitClose.

Two details bite in production. The bridge runs the flow on Dispatchers.Unconfined unless you pass a dispatcher, so the flow and every Reactor operator after it run on whichever thread resumed it: the subscriber's thread at first, kotlinx.coroutines.DefaultExecutor after a delay, and the SDK's own thread under a gateway bridge. Pass asFlux(dispatcher) or add publishOn before anything slow downstream. And Reactor's Context crosses in both directions. Through asFlux(), a traceId written with contextWrite was visible inside the flow as a ReactorContext element. The other way, a ReactorContext in the coroutine reaches a publisher collected with asFlow() only when kotlinx-coroutines-reactor is on the classpath, because that module supplies the injector, found with ServiceLoader.

Java can't call Flow.collect, which it sees as Object collect(FlowCollector, Continuation). Give Java a face built in Kotlin:

Java
// Java caller: only Reactor types, no Flow and no Continuation
List<GatewayEvent> firstTwo = new GatewayApi(gateway).eventsFlux().take(2).collectList().block();
Kotlin
class GatewayApi(private val gateway: FakeGateway) {
    fun events(): Flow<GatewayEvent> = gateway.events()        // for Kotlin callers
    fun eventsFlux(): Flux<GatewayEvent> = events().asFlux()   // for Java and Reactor callers
}

For a finite result, a CompletableFuture built with scope.future { } is the better face, as lesson 11 of the coroutines track showed.

Part 2: after request(2) the subscriber has [1, 2] while emit has returned only for [1]; after request(3) it is [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and [1, 2, 3, 4]. The Java twin shows Reactor's own demand on a Flow-backed Flux: blockLast() asks for MAX, limitRate(10) for 10 and then 8 at a time, publishOn and flatMap for 256 and then 192. It prints the same two lines for request(2) and request(3).

sections.html:
runTest replaces the clock with a scheduler that jumps from one due task to the next (lesson 10 of the coroutines track). Think of a film editor's timeline with the empty stretches cut out. Three calls move along it, and each stops at a different place:

  • runCurrent() plays the current frame: everything due now.
  • advanceTimeBy(n) fast-forwards up to, but not including, now + n. With tasks due at 100 and 200, advanceTimeBy(100) leaves the clock at 100 with fired=[]. Only runCurrent() then runs the task at 100.
  • advanceUntilIdle() fast-forwards until only background work is left. With nothing but a poller in backgroundScope, it leaves t=0 polls=0, while advanceTimeBy(5000) plus runCurrent() gives t=5000 polls=5.

A test that collects a hot flow in backgroundScope should drive the clock with advanceTimeBy(...) and runCurrent(), as this track's labs do. Reactor's virtual clock puts the edge elsewhere:

Java
// Java equivalent: Reactor's VirtualTimeScheduler includes the end point
@Test
void taskDueAt100RunsWithAdvanceTimeBy() {
    VirtualTimeScheduler clock = VirtualTimeScheduler.create();
    List<Long> fired = new ArrayList<>();
    clock.schedule(() -> fired.add(100L), 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
    clock.advanceTimeBy(Duration.ofMillis(100));
    assertThat(fired).containsExactly(100L);  // already ran, no extra step
}
Kotlin
@Test
fun `the task due at 100 needs runCurrent`() = runTest {
    val fired = mutableListOf<Long>()
    launch { delay(100); fired += currentTime }
    advanceTimeBy(100)
    assertThat(fired).isEmpty()               // runs only what is due BEFORE now + 100
    runCurrent()
    assertThat(fired).containsExactly(100L)   // runs what is due now
}

The dispatcher decides what a StateFlow collector sees. authorizeAndCapture() sets AUTHORIZED and then CAPTURED with no suspension between them. A collector on the default StandardTestDispatcher runs only when the test lets it, so it saw [PENDING, CAPTURED]. One launched with UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler), which is experimental, runs inside each set and saw all three. A real collector on Dispatchers.Default can see either. The Unconfined test shows the most a collector can see, and the Standard one shows conflation. Assert on the final state and on the transitions that matter. If every transition matters, the type shouldn't be a StateFlow.

Two failures come with exact messages. async { status.take(3).toList() } waits for a third value that conflation ate, and with runTest(timeout = 500.milliseconds) it ends in UncompletedCoroutinesError: After waiting for 500ms, the test body did not run to completion. (The default timeout is 60 s, and the 20 s JUnit timeout in these labs fires first.) A hot flow collected in the test scope itself, or stateIn(this, WhileSubscribed(), 0), fails with there were active child jobs, followed by the advice to use TestScope.backgroundScope.

try.title: Find the edges of the test clock
steps: Read TestClock.kt. Predict every line before you run it, the two error messages included.
Run it. Parts 4 and 5 each wait 500 ms of real time for the runTest timeout.
In part 1, change advanceTimeBy(100) to advanceTimeBy(101). What does the first line print now?

code.title: TestClock.kt

_status.value = "CAPTURED" } // no suspension between } // The edges of the test clock. runTest is called from main here; in a test it is the body. @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun main() { runTest { println("== 1. advanceTimeBy(n) runs what is due BEFORE now + n") val fired = mutableListOf<Long>() launch { delay(100); fired += currentTime } launch { delay(200); fired += currentTime } advanceTimeBy(100); println(" after advanceTimeBy(100): t=$currentTime fired=$fired") runCurrent(); println(" after runCurrent(): t=$currentTime fired=$fired") advanceUntilIdle(); println(" after advanceUntilIdle(): t=$currentTime fired=$fired") } runTest { println("== 2. advanceUntilIdle() stops once only backgroundScope work is left") var polls = 0 backgroundScope.launch { while (true) { delay(1_000); polls++ } } // a settlement poller advanceUntilIdle(); println(" after advanceUntilIdle(): t=$currentTime polls=$polls") advanceTimeBy(5_000); runCurrent(); println(" after advanceTimeBy(5000) + runCurrent(): t=$currentTime polls=$polls") } runTest { println("== 3. a StateFlow set twice in a row, collected two ways") val a = StatusTracker(); val standard = mutableListOf<String>() backgroundScope.launch { a.status.toList(standard) } runCurrent(); a.authorizeAndCapture(); runCurrent() val b = StatusTracker(); val unconfined = mutableListOf<String>() backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { b.status.toList(unconfined) } b.authorizeAndCapture() println(" Standard collector: $standard") println(" Unconfined collector: $unconfined") } println("== 4. take(3) on that StateFlow (runTest timeout 500 ms of REAL time)") try { runTest(timeout = 500.milliseconds) { val t = StatusTracker() val three = async { t.status.take(3).toList() } runCurrent() t.authorizeAndCapture() println(" got ${three.await()}") } } catch (e: Throwable) { println(" ${e::class.qualifiedName}: ${e.message?.lines()?.first()}") } println("== 5. stateIn(this, WhileSubscribed()) inside runTest, over flowOf(1, 2, 3)") try { runTest(timeout = 500.milliseconds) { val s = flowOf(1, 2, 3).stateIn(this, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(), 0) println(" saw ${s.first { it == 3 }}, test body done") } println(" test passed") } catch (e: Throwable) { println(" ${e::class.qualifiedName}: ${e.message?.lines()?.first()?.replace(Regex("@[0-9a-f]+"), "@...")}") } }

try.expect: Part 1: t=100 fired=[], then fired=[100] after runCurrent(), then t=200 fired=[100, 200]. Part 2: t=0 polls=0, then t=5000 polls=5. Part 3: [PENDING, CAPTURED] for the Standard collector and [PENDING, AUTHORIZED, CAPTURED] for the Unconfined one. Part 4: UncompletedCoroutinesError: After waiting for 500ms, the test body did not run to completion. Part 5 prints saw 3, test body done and then fails with there were active child jobs, because the WhileSubscribed sharing coroutine never ends. With advanceTimeBy(101) the clock stops at 101 and the task at 100 has already run, so the first line reads t=101 fired=[100]. (Reactor's virtual clock has no Java twin here: it lives in reactor-test, which only the tests can use.)

sections.h: Turbine is a stenographer, and it hears everything
sections.html:
Turbine 1.2.1 (app.cash.turbine, a test dependency of this lab module) turns a flow into a transcript you read line by line:

Java
// Java equivalent: StepVerifier subscribes, then runs each step in order
StepVerifier.create(api.eventsFlux())
    .then(() -> gateway.fire(authorized))
    .expectNext(authorized)
    .then(() -> gateway.fail(new IOException("gateway connection lost")))
    .expectErrorMessage("gateway connection lost")
    .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(5));
Kotlin
gateway.events().test {          // collects before the block runs: the listener is registered
    gateway.fire(authorized)
    assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo(authorized)
    gateway.fail(IOException("gateway connection lost"))
    assertThat(awaitError()).hasMessage("gateway connection lost")
}

Picture a court stenographer. test { } runs the flow up to its first suspension before your block starts, so a SharedFlow is subscribed and a callbackFlow listener is registered by then, which removes the race from the first section. Every event goes into the transcript, an unlimited channel, in order. You read it with awaitItem(), awaitComplete() and awaitError(), which hands you the error as an event instead of throwing it. An event you never read fails the test with Unconsumed events found, unless you end with cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents(). If no new line arrives within 3 s of wall-clock time, the test fails with No value produced in 3s. The flow's own delay calls stay virtual inside runTest; only Turbine's wait is real. To follow two flows at once, call testIn(backgroundScope) inside turbineScope { }. Outside it, testIn compiles and then fails at run time with Turbine can only collect flows within a TurbineContext.

The stenographer hears everything, and that is its blind spot. Turbine collects on UnconfinedTestDispatcher, so it takes each value the instant it is sent. It saw AUTHORIZED, which the Standard collector of the last section never got. It also took all 500 events of a burst through a 64-slot callbackFlow, where a Standard collector got 65. Use Turbine to check what a flow emits and in what order. Don't use it to test conflation, buffer sizes or a slow consumer. For those, collect with a Standard collector in backgroundScope and drive the clock yourself, as the lab's burst test does. And on a SharedFlow with no replay, a value emitted before test { } starts is gone, so the test fails with No value produced.

try.title: A tour of Turbine
steps: Read TurbineTourTest.kt. For each of the eight tests, predict the commented line before you run anything.
Run the class with the command below. All eight pass; test 6 waits half a second of real time.
In test 4, delete the line that awaits CAPTURED and run again. Predict the failure message first.

code.title: TurbineTourTest.kt
code.html: package workbench.flows.l08 import app.cash.turbine.test import app.cash.turbine.turbineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.awaitClose import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableSharedFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableStateFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.StateFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.asStateFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.callbackFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flowOf import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.toList import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.reactor.asFlux import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runCurrent import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest import org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import java.io.IOException import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.milliseconds import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds /** A payment whose status is set twice in a row, with no suspension in between. */ class TourTracker { private val _status = MutableStateFlow("PENDING") val status: StateFlow<String> = _status.asStateFlow() fun authorizeAndCapture() { _status.value = "AUTHORIZED"; _status.value = "CAPTURED" } fun statusFlux(): Flux<String> = status.asFlux() // for the Java twin, StepVerifierTourTest } /** * The Try it for Turbine in lesson 8 (not part of the lab): what Turbine sees, and what it hides. * Every test passes. Read each one, predict the commented line, then run the class. */ @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) // TestScope.runCurrent is experimental in 1.11.0 class TurbineTourTest { @Test fun `1 items and completion are awaited in order`() = runTest { flowOf("AUTHORIZED", "CAPTURED").test { assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo("AUTHORIZED") assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo("CAPTURED") awaitComplete() } } @Test fun `2 an event you did not read fails the test`() = runTest { val failure = runCatching { flowOf("one", "two").test { awaitItem() } }.exceptionOrNull() assertThat(failure).hasMessageContaining("Unconsumed events found") // lists Item(two) and Complete } @Test fun `3 an error arrives as an event, not as a thrown exception`() = runTest { flow { emit(1); throw IOException("issuer 503") }.test { assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo(1) assertThat(awaitError()).hasMessage("issuer 503") } } @Test fun `4 Turbine sees every StateFlow value, a Standard collector does not`() = runTest { val tracker = TourTracker() tracker.status.test { assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo("PENDING") tracker.authorizeAndCapture() assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo("AUTHORIZED") // Turbine collects on UnconfinedTestDispatcher assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo("CAPTURED") } val other = TourTracker() val seen = mutableListOf<String>() backgroundScope.launch { other.status.toList(seen) } // StandardTestDispatcher, closer to production runCurrent() other.authorizeAndCapture() runCurrent() assertThat(seen).containsExactly("PENDING", "CAPTURED") } @Test fun `5 Turbine never lets a callbackFlow buffer fill`() = runTest { val gw = FakeGateway() val defaultBuffer: Flow<GatewayEvent> = callbackFlow { // 64 slots, as callbackFlow has by default val r = gw.register(object : GatewayListener { override fun onEvent(event: GatewayEvent) { trySend(event) } override fun onError(error: Throwable) { close(error) } override fun onClosed() { close() } }) awaitClose { r.unregister() } } defaultBuffer.test { gw.burst(500) repeat(500) { awaitItem() } // all 500 arrive: each one was taken the moment it was sent cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents() } val seen = mutableListOf<GatewayEvent>() backgroundScope.launch { defaultBuffer.collect { seen += it } } runCurrent() gw.burst(500) runCurrent() assertThat(seen).hasSize(65) // a Standard collector: 64 buffered plus 1 handed straight over } @Test fun `6 a SharedFlow value emitted before test {} is lost`() = runTest { val events = MutableSharedFlow<String>() events.emit("AUTHORIZED") // nobody is subscribed yet, and replay = 0 val failure = runCatching { events.test(timeout = 500.milliseconds) { awaitItem() } }.exceptionOrNull() assertThat(failure).hasMessage("No value produced in 500ms") // after 500 ms of REAL time } @Test fun `7 the flow's delays are virtual, Turbine's timeout is wall-clock`() = runTest { flow { delay(10.seconds); emit("late") }.test(timeout = 200.milliseconds) { assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo("late") awaitComplete() } } @Test fun `8 several flows at once with turbineScope and testIn`() = runTest { turbineScope { val rates = flowOf(1.0850, 1.0851).testIn(backgroundScope, name = "rates") val alerts = flowOf("drift").testIn(backgroundScope, name = "alerts") assertThat(rates.awaitItem()).isEqualTo(1.0850) assertThat(alerts.awaitItem()).isEqualTo("drift") assertThat(rates.awaitItem()).isEqualTo(1.0851) rates.awaitComplete() alerts.awaitComplete() } } }

} @Test @DisplayName("2. a signal you did not expect fails the test") void unexpectedSignal() { AssertionError failure = assertThrows(AssertionError.class, () -> StepVerifier.create(Flux.just("one", "two")).expectNext("one").expectComplete().verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1))); try.expect: All eight pass. Turbine reads items and completion in order, reports an unread event as Unconsumed events found, and hands the error over as an event. It sees all three StateFlow values where the Standard collector sees [PENDING, CAPTURED], and takes all 500 burst events where the Standard collector gets 65. It misses the value emitted before test { }, with No value produced in 500ms, and a virtual 10 s delay passes inside a 200 ms timeout. With the CAPTURED line gone, test 4 fails with Unconsumed events found, listing Item(CAPTURED). The Java twin passes six StepVerifier tests: an unexpected signal fails with actual: onNext(two), a Kotlin StateFlow through asFlux() delivers all three values as Turbine does, a hot item emitted before anyone subscribed is lost and verify times out, and thenAwait of 10 s runs the task due at exactly +10 s.

refs.title: Testing Kotlin flows (Android developers): the StateFlow conflation warning

analogy: A callbackFlow is a mailbox bolted to an SDK's front door. The SDK's van drops letters through the slot with trySend; the box holds 64, and one more goes straight into a hand that is already waiting. awaitClose is you on the porch, ready to unscrew the box when you're told to leave. The Reactor bridge is a restaurant order pad: the Kotlin diner orders 64 plates and orders again after eating 64, while Reactor's waiter orders n, and the Kotlin cook serves each plate the moment it is ready and stops mid-motion when the order runs out. The test scheduler is a film editor's timeline with the empty stretches cut, and Turbine is a stenographer who writes down every word. The analogy breaks at the stenographer. A real one can only write as fast as people speak, but Turbine takes every value the instant it is sent, which is why it can't show you what a slower listener would miss.
world: Most payment SDKs you wrap have a listener API: a card-gateway client with onEvent and onError, a webhook dispatcher, a settlement-file watcher. Each becomes a callbackFlow with awaitClose and a buffer sized for the burst its documentation promises on reconnect, with failed trySend results counted in a metric so that a loss is visible. When Java code in the same Quarkus or Spring application calls that Kotlin service, give it a Flux built with asFlux() (with a dispatcher if the operators after it are slow, because otherwise they run on the SDK's thread) or a CompletableFuture for a finite answer, and never a Flow. In the tests, inject the dispatcher, wait for the registration before firing events, collect hot flows in backgroundScope, and keep Turbine for content and order, with a Standard collector for anything about timing or buffers.
mistake: The most common mistake is a callbackFlow test that fires an event right after launching the collector: backgroundScope.launch { gateway.events().collect { got += it } }, then gateway.fire(event). On the default StandardTestDispatcher the collector hasn't run, its producer hasn't registered, and the event goes nowhere; afterwards got is empty and the listener count is 1. People then add a delay or switch every test to Unconfined, and the second fix can hide a buffer that is too small. Make the registration explicit instead: call runCurrent() after the launch and assert the listener count, or use Turbine's test { }, which registers before its block runs. Production has the same gap, so code that fires events right after it starts collecting needs its own signal that the listener is in place.

compare.title: A gateway bridge: Flux.create next to callbackFlow

java.title: GatewayEvents.java (Reactor)
java.html: static Flux<GatewayEvent> events(FakeGateway gateway) { return Flux.<GatewayEvent>create(sink -> { Registration registration = gateway.register(new GatewayListener() { @Override public void onEvent(GatewayEvent e) { sink.next(e); } // runs the subscriber inline @Override public void onError(Throwable t) { sink.error(t); } @Override public void onClosed() { sink.complete(); } }); sink.onDispose(registration::unregister); // optional: nothing complains if it is missing }) .onBackpressureBuffer(500); // the default buffer has no limit }

kotlin.title: GatewayEvents.kt (callbackFlow)
kotlin.html: fun FakeGateway.events(): Flow<GatewayEvent> = callbackFlow { val registration = register(object : GatewayListener { override fun onEvent(event: GatewayEvent) { trySend(event) } // never blocks the SDK thread override fun onError(error: Throwable) { close(error) } override fun onClosed() { close() } }) awaitClose { registration.unregister() } // required: collecting throws without it }.buffer(500) // fused into the bridge's channel; the default is 64

compare.note: The shapes match line for line, and four things differ. Registration time: Flux.create registers inside subscribe(), while callbackFlow registers when its producer coroutine first runs, so an event fired right after collect starts can be lost. Cleanup: callbackFlow throws when its block returns without awaitClose, and Reactor lets a missing onDispose leak the listener with no message. Buffering: Kotlin's channel holds 64 (65 with a waiting receiver) and makes you look at trySend's result; Reactor buffers without limit unless you add a policy. Threads: sink.next calls the subscriber's onNext on the SDK's thread, while the Kotlin collector runs on its own dispatcher and the SDK thread only drops the event into the channel. That holds until you turn the flow into a Flux with plain asFlux(), whose Unconfined default puts the subscriber back on the SDK's thread.

worked.title: Hand the gateway to Java, and test it from both sides

steps.say: Start from the Kotlin bridge, the lab's solution. It registers per collector, never blocks the SDK thread, closes the channel on onError and onClosed, and has room for the 500-event replay.
steps.code: fun FakeGateway.events(): Flow<GatewayEvent> = callbackFlow { val registration = register(object : GatewayListener { override fun onEvent(event: GatewayEvent) { trySend(event) } // 1. hand over, never block override fun onError(error: Throwable) { close(error) } // 2. fail the flow override fun onClosed() { close() } // 3. complete it }) awaitClose { registration.unregister() } // 4. clean up on any ending }.buffer(500)

alt.html: // Java equivalent of the same four steps static Flux<GatewayEvent> events(FakeGateway gateway) { return Flux.<GatewayEvent>create(sink -> { Registration registration = gateway.register(new GatewayListener() { @Override public void onEvent(GatewayEvent e) { sink.next(e); } // 1. @Override public void onError(Throwable t) { sink.error(t); } // 2. @Override public void onClosed() { sink.complete(); } // 3. }); sink.onDispose(registration::unregister); // 4. }).onBackpressureBuffer(500); }

steps.say: Give Java a face. asFlux() starts the flow at the first request(n), so registration happens then and not at subscribe(). A cancelled subscription cancels the flow, so awaitClose unregisters.
steps.code: class GatewayApi(private val gateway: FakeGateway) { fun events(): Flow<GatewayEvent> = gateway.events() fun eventsFlux(): Flux<GatewayEvent> = gateway.events().asFlux() // Unconfined: pass a dispatcher if operators after it are slow }

steps.say: Test the content with Turbine and the buffer with a Standard collector. Turbine registers before its block runs and reads events in order. The burst test needs a collector that can't run during the burst, so it uses the default dispatcher and runCurrent().

lab.title: Bridge a gateway listener, hand it to Java, test it both ways
steps: Run the tests. The five GatewayEventsTest cases and the three in GatewayFluxTest (a Java test) fail. TurbineTourTest and StepVerifierTourTest already pass: they are this lesson's Try it. Read one failure: it is the awaitClose message from the first section.

In GatewayEvents.kt, keep the Registration that register returns, close the channel from onError and onClosed, and end the block with awaitClose. Run GatewayEventsTest. One test still fails, with a number you have seen in this lesson.
Size the bridge's channel for the 500-event replay the KDoc promises, without blocking the SDK's thread.
In GatewayApi.kt, write eventsFlux(). Run GatewayFluxTest, which sees only Reactor types.
Run all the l08 tests. Then read GatewayEventsTest and say, for each test, why it uses Turbine, an Unconfined collector or a Standard one.
hints: close(error) and close() belong to the ProducerScope the block runs in, so you can call them from inside the listener object.

Expected size: 500 but was: 65 is the default 64 slots plus the one event handed to the waiting collector. A buffer(...) right after callbackFlow { } is fused into its channel. Channel.UNLIMITED passes too; a number states how much memory you allow.
Don't reach for trySendBlocking. In the burst test the SDK's thread is the test's only thread, the one the collector needs in order to run.
asFlux() is in kotlinx.coroutines.reactor. It starts the flow at the first request(n) and cancels it when the subscription is cancelled, which is what the Java tests check.

drill.title: A listener bridge, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. A made-up webhook SDK has fun subscribe(onDelivery: (Delivery) -> Unit, onFailure: (Throwable) -> Unit): Cancellable. Write fun WebhookSdk.deliveries(): Flow<Delivery> that never blocks the SDK's thread, fails the flow on onFailure, holds a burst of 1,000 deliveries, and cancels the SDK subscription whatever ends the collection. Then say in a comment what happens if you leave out the cleanup line.

answer.html: fun WebhookSdk.deliveries(): Flow<Delivery> = callbackFlow { val subscription = subscribe( onDelivery = { delivery -> trySend(delivery) }, // never blocks the SDK thread onFailure = { error -> close(error) }, // collect throws this error ) awaitClose { subscription.cancel() } // on take(n), cancellation, close and error }.buffer(1_000) // fused into the callbackFlow's channel // Without awaitClose the block returns with the channel open, and collecting throws // IllegalStateException: 'awaitClose { yourCallbackOrListener.cancel() }' should be used // in the end of callbackFlow block.

alt.title: Java equivalent
alt.html: // Java equivalent, for an SDK whose Java API is subscribe(Consumer<Delivery>, Consumer<Throwable>) Flux<Delivery> deliveries(WebhookSdk sdk) { return Flux.<Delivery>create(sink -> { Cancellable subscription = sdk.subscribe(sink::next, sink::error); sink.onDispose(subscription::cancel); // leave it out and the subscription leaks, silently }).onBackpressureBuffer(1_000); // caps the default unlimited buffer }

recap: callbackFlow registers when its producer coroutine first runs, after collect starts, so an event fired in between is lost. Tests wait for the registration; Turbine's test { } does it for you. Reactor's Flux.create registers inside subscribe().

awaitClose { unregister() } runs on take(n), cancellation, close(error) and close(). Without it, collecting throws the exact IllegalStateException shown in the lesson. Use channelFlow for your own coroutines and suspendCancellableCoroutine for a one-shot callback.

The bridge holds 64 by default plus one handed to a waiting receiver, so 65 of a 200-event burst got in. Check trySend's result, and choose a fused buffer(n), conflate() or UNLIMITED (for a bounded producer) on purpose. trySendBlocking blocks the SDK's thread.

Publisher.asFlow() requests 64, then 64 more after each 64; buffer(n) makes it request(n). asFlux() starts at the first request, calls onNext inside emit and suspends there when demand runs out, on Unconfined unless you pass a dispatcher. Give Java a Flux or a CompletableFuture, never a Flow.

advanceTimeBy(n) runs what is due before now + n, runCurrent() what is due now, and advanceUntilIdle() stops when only backgroundScope work is left. A Standard collector shows StateFlow conflation; an Unconfined one shows every value.

Turbine reads a flow like a transcript with a 3 s wall-clock timeout. It collects on UnconfinedTestDispatcher, so it can't show conflation or a buffer that is too small: test those with a Standard collector and the clock.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate why gateway.fire(e) right after backgroundScope.launch { gateway.events().collect { ... } } loses the event in a test, why rewriting the test with Turbine fixes that, and why Turbine would then hide a buffer that is too small.
explain.answer: On the default StandardTestDispatcher, launch only queues the collector. The callbackFlow's producer coroutine, which calls register, runs the next time the scheduler runs, so the fire happens with no listener and the event goes nowhere. Turbine's test { } runs the flow up to its first suspension before the block starts, so by then the listener is registered. But Turbine collects on UnconfinedTestDispatcher. Each trySend resumes it at once and the event leaves the channel right away, so the channel never fills, and a 64-slot buffer passes a 500-event burst. To test the buffer, collect with a Standard collector that can't run during the burst: launch it, call runCurrent() so it registers, fire the burst, call runCurrent() again and count.

deeper.html:
The JDK has its own Reactive Streams interfaces, java.util.concurrent.Flow, with Publisher, Subscriber and Subscription. kotlinx.coroutines bridges them in a separate artifact, org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-jdk9:1.11.0. It is a thin wrapper over the reactive module: asFlow(), asPublisher() and collect for the JDK types, with the same demand mapping (a JDK publisher over 150 items saw request(64) three times). You don't need the extra artifact. reactive-streams 1.0.4, already on this lab's classpath through kotlinx-coroutines-reactive, has org.reactivestreams.FlowAdapters, and FlowAdapters.toPublisher(jdkPublisher).asFlow() does the same job.

The JDK HttpClient shows why that matters. client.sendAsync(request, BodyHandlers.ofPublisher()) is two bridges in one call. The CompletableFuture completes once, when the headers arrive, so it belongs to await(). The body is a JDK Flow.Publisher<List<ByteBuffer>> that delivers chunks as they come off the socket, so it belongs to asFlow(). In one run against a local server that wrote five lines 50 ms apart, the chunks arrived about 50 ms apart too. Wrapping the future in callbackFlow would be the wrong tool: a single result is a suspendCancellableCoroutine or await() job.

A few facts about the Reactor modules themselves. The README of kotlinx-coroutines-reactive calls asPublisher TCK-compliant. The subscription it creates has no parent job, so its lifetime belongs to the subscription and not to any scope. Element types must be non-null (T : Any), because Reactive Streams forbids null items. And the 1.11.0 reactor module declares reactor-core 3.4.1 in its pom; this course pins 3.8.8, and Gradle picks the higher version.
